short_description: Volume I of a two volume series. Bayesian clinical trials built up from the traditional trial and tied to regulation: calibration, monitoring, safety, borrowing, adaptive designs, and reanalyses of landmark trials, with an R package and an online lab.
description:
This book is for the people who run clinical trials: investigators, physicians, biostatisticians at sponsors and contract research organizations, data monitoring committee members, and regulatory reviewers. It assumes an introductory statistics course and nothing more.

The book starts from the traditional trial, with a fixed sample size, equal randomization, alpha spending for interim looks, and a p value and confidence interval in the study report. It then shows the Bayesian version of the same decision on the same numbers, and says plainly where the traditional design is the better choice. Regulation is the spine: each chapter names the statute, regulation or guidance that governs its topic, with its status and date.

Our main claim is that a Bayesian adaptive design reaches the regulatory standard of evidence sooner without lowering the bar. Against a single unadjusted look the Bayesian bar is never lower without an informative prior. The saving comes from monitoring, from the handling of multiple arms, and from prior information, and we price each one with calibrated rules and simulated operating characteristics.

We test this on real trials. In our reconstruction of the semaglutide trial SELECT, simulated at a true hazard ratio of 0.80, a calibrated Bayesian rule stops at a median of 486 events over all simulated trials (464 among those that declare efficacy), against 817 for SELECT's planned design (one interim analysis with Lan-DeMets spending, then the final), with power of 95 percent against 97 percent; an anytime valid evidence rule is slower and less powerful. The reconstruction is ours, not the sponsor's. We also put the cost of waiting in three currencies, the trial cost avoided, the cardiovascular label reached earlier inside a fixed patent life, and the health value inside and outside the trial, each a modeled counterfactual with its assumptions stated. A scheduled design can win when the effect is modest, as the dulaglutide trial REWIND shows.

Beyond design and monitoring, the book follows a drug from first in human to postmarketing, with recruitment and the value of speed told through the 1995 Larry King appeal for prostate cancer families, covers covariate adjustment, safety signals (rofecoxib, the gamma Poisson shrinker, toxicity stopping rules), time to event endpoints, noninferiority, Bayesian reanalyses of GUSTO, EOLIA, ANDROMEDA SHOCK and RECOVERY, and trials running now, among them TRIUMPH 3 and Lp(a)HORIZON. Volume II of the series turns to personalized medicine.

Every number comes from the companion R package bayestrials (https://github.com/VadimSokolov/bayestrials), an interactive lab at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/ lets readers run the trials themselves, and an online encyclopedia at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/encyclopedia/ links the methods, trials and documents to the sections of the book that treats it.

chapters.title: A Trial Is a Decision
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what a clinical trial is for. It opens with SELECT, the semaglutide cardiovascular outcomes trial, and a ledger of what such a trial costs in patients, money and time, then argues that trialists should want a Bayesian approach because of the price of a trial, of being wrong and of waiting, and reviews evidence on how much efficiency real adaptive and Bayesian trials achieved and whether the approach is spreading. A counterweight section states the strongest objections. The chapter states the traditional trial fairly: a fixed sample size from a power calculation, randomization, alpha spending for interim looks, a multiplicity correction and a p-value in the clinical study report, together with what that apparatus costs. It then recasts the same choice as a decision, where a prior, a utility and a rule say when acting beats waiting, and shows that with a flat prior and one look the Bayesian rule is the one sided test. It previews the thesis and four mechanisms (the deviation scale, a single calibrated threshold with shrinkage, informative priors and optimal stopping), says what the regulator needs and does not need, gives a short history and maps the book. It proves nothing new; it fixes the vocabulary and the claim that the saving comes from monitoring, multiplicity and prior information and not from a lower bar.

#### From the literature

The probability that one treatment is better and allocation by it (Thompson 1933); sequential analysis (Wald 1947); the economics of experimentation (Grundy, Healy and Rees 1956); preposterior analysis and decision theory (Raiffa and Schlaifer 1961); trials as decisions for future patients (Anscombe 1963, Colton 1963); sequential boundaries (O'Brien and Fleming 1979, Lan and DeMets 1983); Bayesian interim monitoring (Berry 1985, Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994); the SELECT trial (Lincoff and colleagues 2023, Ryan and colleagues 2020); trial costs (Sertkaya and colleagues 2016, Moore and colleagues 2018, 2020); adaptive efficiencies (Saville and Berry 2016); BNT162b2 (Polack and colleagues 2020); REMAP-CAP (Gordon and colleagues 2021); RECOVERY; substantial evidence of effectiveness (FD&C Act section 505(d), 21 CFR 314.126); ICH E8(R1), E9 and E9(R1); the FDA draft on Bayesian methodology (January 2026) and the EMA concept paper (2025).

chapters.title: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV
chapters.summary:
This chapter walks through the life of a drug, Phase I to IV, and asks at each phase which decision is made and with what evidence. Phase I looks for safety and a dose, Phase II for signs of activity and the dose to carry forward, Phase III for confirmation and the regulatory decision, and Phase IV for what appears after approval. The chapter treats the phases as a sequence of options, where each phase buys information that is worth having only if it can change the next decision. It covers bioequivalence by two one sided tests (TOST) and a posterior summary, and then reads the phases in Bayesian terms: what a prior from one phase becomes in the next, and where the traditional separation of phases hides information. The rofecoxib story (VIGOR, APPROVe) appears as a Phase IV lesson on safety that a trial too small for harm cannot see. It proves nothing new.

#### From the literature

Dose escalation with overdose control (Babb, Rogatko and Zacks 1998); the continual reassessment method (O'Quigley, Pepe and Fisher 1990); Bayesian logistic regression for dose finding (Neuenschwander, Branson and Gsponer 2008); two stage bioequivalence (Racine Poon and colleagues 1987); decision analysis for bioequivalence (Lindley 1998); learning versus confirming in drug development (Sheiner 1997); the TGN1412 cytokine storm in a phase 1 trial (Suntharalingam and colleagues 2006); equivalence and bioequivalence (Westlake 1976, Schuirmann 1987, Hauck and Anderson 1984, Selwyn and colleagues 1981, Rodda and Davis 1980, Mandallaz and Mau 1981, Fluhler and colleagues 1983); the ASTIN stroke dose trial (Krams and colleagues 2003); the VIGOR and APPROVe rofecoxib trials (Bombardier and colleagues 2000, Bresalier and colleagues 2005) and their reanalysis (Juni and colleagues 2004); Bayesian signal detection (DuMouchel 1999); phase transition success rates (Wong, Siah and Lo 2019); FDA bioequivalence statistics guidance (2026).

chapters.title: The Regulatory Framework
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains the legal and regulatory frame in which a trial is designed. It begins with the statutory standard of substantial evidence in section 505(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the 1997 amendment that allows one trial with confirmatory evidence, the regulation 21 CFR 314.126 on what adequate and well controlled means, and the 2026 draft on substantial evidence. It describes what a traditional submission looks like and what changes with a Bayesian adaptive design. It then goes through the ICH principles (E3, E6(R3), E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E11A, E20, M4, M15), the FDA design guidances (adaptive designs, master protocols, multiple endpoints, optimizing dosage, external controls, AI credibility), the history of Bayesian methods at the regulators before 2026 and the January 2026 FDA draft on Bayesian methodology with the response to it. It separates what the documents require, recommend and permit, describes how to interact with FDA (PDUFA meetings, the Complex Innovative Trial Design and MIDD paired meeting programs, CPIM, drug development tool qualification), and gives the EMA and MHRA counterparts. Case studies include REBYOTA, BNT162b2, pediatric belimumab, and the devices Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart.

chapters.title: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up
chapters.summary:
This chapter builds the comparison of two treatments from the ground up with simulated and real trial data. It starts with one trial and two endpoints, reruns it many times, and derives the randomization test, the normal approximation and the z test. It defines the p-value carefully, explains confidence intervals and their duality with tests, and defines type I error, type II error and power. It explains why a one sided level of 0.025 is used, and covers noninferiority and equivalence against a margin, with the SURPASS CVOT noninferiority margin as an example. It closes with where the traditional trial stands and what changes next. Examples are RECOVERY (a rate ratio and an interval) and ANDROMEDA SHOCK (what not significant does and does not mean). The chapter proves nothing new; it sets down the traditional machinery that later chapters compare against.

chapters.title: Randomization From the Ground Up
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks why trials randomize and what randomization buys. It sets out the counterfactual problem and confounding by indication, what goes wrong without randomization, and the methods: simple, permuted block, stratified randomization and minimization, with how a schedule is actually generated and why allocation must be concealed. It develops randomization inference, discusses what randomness is (incompressibility and Kolmogorov complexity, and Arnold's measure), blinding, and intention to treat with the estimands framework and intercurrent events. It then asks why a Bayesian still randomizes, through ignorability of the assignment mechanism and the Bayesian arguments for randomizing. A long section covers covariate adjustment: ANCOVA, change from baseline, analyzing as you randomized, not testing baseline balance, binary and time to event outcomes, estimators robust to model misspecification, what FDA and EMA say, and the Bayesian version. It ends with what the protocol should state. Case studies are the MRC streptomycin trial, RECOVERY and the Women's Health Initiative.

chapters.title: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
chapters.summary:
This chapter introduces Bayesian inference through the same kinds of trials as before. It starts with Bayes' rule on a diagnostic test, exchangeability and de Finetti informally, and the coin with the Beta family. It shows the posterior mean as a weighted average and the prior's effective sample size, then redoes the two group comparison in traditional and Bayesian form, side by side, and explains why the two nearly agree. It compares credible and confidence intervals, introduces the posterior predictive distribution, and works the normal normal model on the log hazard ratio. It shows sequential updating, where the posterior today is the prior tomorrow, and that looking at the data does not change the posterior. It closes with what a protocol must say. Two trials that stated their success rule as a posterior probability are discussed: Pfizer and BioNTech BNT162b2 and REMAP-CAP. The chapter proves nothing new.

#### From the literature

Bayes' rule and the likelihood principle (Savage 1954, Edwards, Lindman and Savage 1963, Berger and Wolpert 1988, Berger 1985, Lindley 1985); Bayesian data analysis (Gelman and colleagues 2013); the BNT162b2 phase 3 trial (Polack and colleagues 2020, Pfizer statistical analysis plan 2020, FDA EUA review 2021); REMAP-CAP (Gordon and colleagues 2021); Morita, Thall and Muller (2008) on effective sample size; ICH E9 and E20; the FDA draft guidance on Bayesian methodology (2026).

#### New results

- [Reproduction of the BNT162b2 beta binomial analysis](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#bnt162b2_beta_binomial_reproduction) (Section 6.12.1, page 136; computed): The statistical analysis plan's beta binomial model with a Beta(0.700102, 1) prior, applied to 8 versus 162 cases, gives a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent of 1 minus 2e-28 and a point estimate of 95 per cent, matching the published interval within a tenth of a point. New in this book.

chapters.title: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how much evidence a result carries. It defines the p-value, reviews the ASA statement and the dirty dozen of misinterpretations, and develops the false positive risk. It compares the exact p-value with the Bayes factor, with a Gaussian example in closed form and Lindley's paradox, and asks how small a Bayes factor can be, which gives calibrations of the p-value. It then asks how much evidence is enough on three scales, shows that a test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss, and gives the Bayes risk of a test, what a fixed level implies as information grows, the type I error of the Bayes rule, and the Jeffreys table in terms of a threshold. It moves from p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit, including the FDA success criterion, the flat prior case where Bayes and the p-value agree, and how an informative prior changes the mapping. It compares four quantities side by side. Examples: EOLIA, ANDROMEDA SHOCK and false positive risk in practice (Zia and colleagues).

#### From the literature

The ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016) and the dirty dozen (Goodman 2008); false discoveries and the false positive risk (Soric 1989, Sterne and Davey Smith 2001, Wacholder and colleagues 2004, Ioannidis 2005, Colquhoun 2014, 2017); calibration of p-values (Berger and Sellke 1987, Sellke, Bayarri and Berger 2001, Johnson 2013); Bayes factors (Jeffreys 1935, 1939, Kass and Raftery 1995, Goodman 1999); Lindley's paradox (Lindley 1957, Bartlett 1957); information (Lindley 1956); the Schwarz criterion (1978); redefining statistical significance (Benjamin and colleagues 2018); Bayesianly justifiable and relevant frequency calculations (Rubin 1984); EOLIA (Combes and colleagues 2018, Goligher and colleagues 2018); ANDROMEDA SHOCK (Hernandez and colleagues 2019, Zampieri and colleagues 2020, 2021); Zia and colleagues (2005); Wijeysundera and colleagues (2009); Lewis and Berry (1994); the FDA Bayesian draft (2026).

chapters.title: Choosing and Defending Priors
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats the prior. It begins with the fact that the traditional design has no stated prior but does carry an implicit one, describes where priors come from in a sponsor's program (including the phase 2 selection problem), and gives skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors. It shows why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters, through independent beta priors on the risk difference and flat priors on logistic coefficients, and introduces the conditional means prior. It measures how much a prior weighs by effective sample size, treats prior data conflict and robust priors, and gives sensitivity analysis over the prior scale, including the tipping point prior. It then reads what the FDA draft says, including the device precedent, compares the protocol side by side with the traditional one, shows how to write the prior into the protocol and what can go wrong. Cases are pediatric belimumab in lupus, REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials, EOLIA and BNT162b2.

chapters.title: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
chapters.summary:
This chapter turns to power and sample size. It gives the textbook calculation for binary, continuous and time to event endpoints, its sensitivity to the design alternative and the power curve, and what the regulator sees. It then shows that a conventional power calculation is assurance under a point mass prior, derives a closed form, states what assurance is not, and reviews Bayesian sample size criteria. A long section develops the moderate deviation sample size: the fixed n test has no memory of n, the power function and sample size equation, a surprising result about the saving, the role of prior odds in the constant, many parameters and endpoints, and a reading of SELECT against the formulas, with a candid statement of where the saving is and is not. It continues with sizing for the population in the sense of Anscombe and Colton. Cases: what a sample size costs, SELECT, why the phase 2 design alternative is too large, and platform arithmetic.

#### From the literature

Sample size for survival (Freedman 1982, Schoenfeld 1981, 1983) and the SampleSizeProportions package (Joseph and colleagues 2023); trial size as a decision for the future population (Anscombe 1963, Colton 1963); assurance and Bayesian power (O'Hagan, Stevens and Campbell 2005, Spiegelhalter and Freedman 1986, Crisp and colleagues 2018, Kunzmann and colleagues 2021); Bayesian sample size (Adcock 1988, 1997, Joseph and colleagues 1995, 1997, Lindley 1997, Chaloner and Verdinelli 1995, Pezeshk 2003, Sahu and Smith 2006, Brutti and De Santis 2008, Joseph and colleagues 2019 consensus); the cost of trials (Moore and colleagues 2018, 2020, Saville and Berry 2016); SELECT (Ryan and colleagues 2020, Lincoff and colleagues 2023); the FDA Bayesian draft and ICH E9, E9(R1).

#### New results

- [Moderate deviation sample size equation](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#moderate_deviation_sample_size) (Section 9.3.2, page 202; proved): A Bayes rule whose bar grows like the logarithm of the sample size has an implicit sample size equation, the textbook formula with the critical value replaced by the square root of log n plus a constant. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
- [Moderate deviation and textbook sizes at the SELECT hazard ratio of 0.80 (not a prediction of SELECT's size)](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#moderate_deviation_select_comparison) (Section 9.3.6, page 207; computed): At a hazard ratio of 0.80 and 90 per cent power the textbook formula gives 844 events and the moderate deviation formula more; SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83, where the textbook formula gives about 1,211 events against the planned 1,225, so the formula does not predict SELECT's size. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.

#### Key terms

chapters.title: Multiplicity and Shrinkage
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what multiplicity is and how to pay for it. It starts with many chances for luck and what counts as the family, then the traditional toolbox: Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg, closed testing, fixed sequence and graphical procedures, and what the FDA multiple endpoints guidance asks for. It discusses subgroups and forking paths, and why a Bayesian must also ask how the result was chosen. The Bayesian alternative is shrinkage instead of threshold inflation: the idea, Stein, Efron and Morris and the batting averages, a numerical illustration of the winner's curse, and what shrinkage does not do. It treats false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg) and prior probabilities, where familywise control is not the target, and the Bayesian view of multiplicity, then a large trial with many subgroups (RECOVERY). It works through the four operation ulcer trial, compares the two ways to pay for looking, and extends to platforms across arms and drugs. Cases: I-SPY 2, REMAP-CAP and the FDA master protocol position.

#### From the literature

Bonferroni and Dunn (1961); Holm (1979); Hochberg (1988); Hommel (1988); Simes (1986); closed testing (Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel 1976); gatekeeping (Dmitrienko and colleagues 2003); graphical procedures (Bretz and colleagues 2009, 2011, Burman and colleagues 2009, Maurer and Bretz 2013); false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995, Benjamini and Yekutieli 2001); shrinkage (Stein 1956, James and Stein 1961, Efron and Morris 1975, 1977); empirical Bayes and large scale inference (Efron 2008); Bayesian multiplicity (Berry and Berry 2004, Scott and Berger 2006, 2010, Berry and Hochberg 1999, Gelman and colleagues 2012); type S and M errors (Gelman and Tuerlinckx 2000); subgroups (Wang and colleagues 2007, Rothman 1990, Mehrotra and colleagues 2012); ISIS 2 (1988); I-SPY 2 (Park and colleagues 2016); REMAP-CAP (Gordon and colleagues 2021); the FDA multiple endpoints guidance (2022).

chapters.title: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how to look at accumulating data without losing control of the error. It shows why repeated testing at a fixed level fails, develops the Armitage recursion, and compares O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock and the families between them, plus other boundary families (Armitage plans, the triangular test and designs with futility boundaries). It covers spending functions and the information fraction, futility boundaries (binding and non binding), and what a data monitoring committee does. The Bayesian sequential problem follows: the posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, a short history of Bayesian monitoring, the Bayes sequential decision problem, and Wald's test with its large deviation ledger. The chapter then develops the three deviation scales and their tolls, where the surcharge comes from, the seventy percent result, four boundaries compared and a sequential power calculation. It compares traditional and Bayesian monitoring side by side, runs one outcomes trial under three rulebooks, and gives a reporting template for the monitoring committee. Cases: truncated trials overestimate (Bassler and colleagues), heparin in Covid 19, the EOLIA futility stop and the Women's Health Initiative stop for harm.

#### From the literature

Sequential analysis (Wald 1945, 1948, Barnard 1946); sequential medical plans (Armitage 1954, 1960, Armitage, McPherson and Rowe 1969); stopping rules and optional stopping (Peto and colleagues 1976, Haybittle 1971, Pocock 1977, O'Brien and Fleming 1979); spending functions (Lan and DeMets 1983, Kim and DeMets 1987); triangular test (Whitehead 1983); futility and symmetric designs (Pampallona and Tsiatis 1994, Emerson and Fleming 1989, Kittelson and Emerson 1999); stochastic curtailment (Lan, Simon and Halperin 1982); Jennison and Turnbull (2000); Bayesian monitoring (Berry 1985, Berry 1987, Freedman, Lowe and Macaskill 1984, Freedman and Spiegelhalter 1989, Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994, Grossman and colleagues 1994); the stopping rule principle (Edwards, Lindman and Savage 1963, Berger and Wolpert 1988); truncated trials (Bassler and colleagues 2010, Montori and colleagues 2005, Freidlin and Korn 2009); FDA guidance on data monitoring committees (2006, 2024); EOLIA (Combes and colleagues 2018, Goligher and colleagues 2018); the heparin trials (Goligher and colleagues 2021, Lawler and colleagues 2021); the WHI (Rossouw and colleagues 2002).

#### New results

- [The three deviation scales (evidence tolls)](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#evidence_tolls_three_scales) (Section 11.9.2, page 253; proved): A fixed level test, a Bayes rule and an anytime valid rule act at three different sizes of the squared standardized score; for the normal mixture the anytime valid bar exceeds the Bayes bar by a surcharge that is about 2 log(1/alpha) at large information. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
- [The surcharge for validity at every stopping time is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement, as a comparison of boundary terms](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#surcharge_seventy_percent) (Section 11.9.4, page 256; proved): For the normal mixture e value rule, against the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar (posterior odds of one), the large information surcharge 7.38 is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial standardized requirement 10.51; this compares boundary terms and is not an exact sample size identity. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.

chapters.title: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what validity at every stopping time requires, and what it costs. It begins with what a group sequential design does not cover (unplanned looks and continuous monitoring), then defines e-values as bets, test martingales and Ville's inequality, a betting martingale for a binary endpoint, the growth rate (how big a bet), and the odds of Cornfield in 1966. It covers likelihood ratio, mixture and process e-values (sequences of e-values indexed by time), passes from e-values to p-values and confidence sequences, and states the surcharge that validity at every stopping time costs. It relates e-values to Bayes factors, compares the power and stopping time of e-value, Bayesian and group sequential designs on a two arm binary design and a time to event design reconstructed from SELECT, and explains why the orderings differ. It adds a Bayes risk comparison, asks when a sponsor should pay the surcharge, shows a negative result for the mixture e-value with many subgroups at once, and gives what the regulator will ask. The case is BNT162b2, which had several interim looks on a schedule fixed in the statistical analysis plan.

chapters.title: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats safety, where the question is whether harm is present and what to do about it. It starts with the rofecoxib cumulative signal: what the traditional analysis said, what a Bayesian reading adds, a move from inference to decision, and the naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison. It treats continuous monitoring with a posterior probability and an e-value, signals in spontaneous reports (the traditional proportional reporting measure and the gamma Poisson shrinker), toxicity monitoring inside a trial (the traditional counterpart, the Bayesian rule and operating characteristics), and aggregate safety assessment, which joins blinded pooled review, unblinded committee review, hierarchical models across adverse event terms and surveillance by a maximized sequential probability ratio test. It connects the two views and says what the regulator will ask.

chapters.title: Operating Characteristics by Simulation
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how a Bayesian design earns an error rate. It first describes what a traditional design computes and what goes in the SAP (the fixed sample design and the group sequential design), then the Bayesian success rule and why it has no error rate until calibrated, and why the uncalibrated rule inflates the error. It gives the calibration of the threshold and the interim boundary by simulation, with the algorithm and how to choose them, and a worked two arm binary trial with four looks: type I error across the null space, the null boundary, power, expected sample size, early stopping and bias, and the sources of calibration noise. It covers scenario grids and the worst case, the Goldilocks design, what the simulation report must contain, and software, reproducibility and what to submit. Cases: BNT162b2, REBYOTA, DAWN and Superion.

chapters.title: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks when to stop for futility or success, and what the best rule is. It begins with the traditional interim: conditional power, futility rules, and sample size reestimation with the promising zone. It introduces predictive probability of success, from conditional power to the normal case, the exact beta binomial computation and a time to event example. It reviews the traditional phase 2 design (Simon's two stage design) where Bayesian monitoring started, predictive probability monitoring for phase 2, what that design is and is not, and the economic threshold. It describes the Goldilocks design with two predictive probabilities, then the Bayes optimal rule by backward induction: the decision problem, the sufficient statistic reduction, what backward induction does and does not do, and a single arm example. It compares designs, shows the protocol side by side and gives the regulatory reading. Cases: CALGB 49907, I-SPY 2, DAWN, BNT162b2 and GBM AGILE.

#### From the literature

Conditional power and curtailment (Lan, Simon and Halperin 1982, Halperin and colleagues 1982, Lan and Wittes 1988, Proschan and Hunsberger 1995); predictive power (Herson 1979, Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Blackburn 1986, Johns and Anderson 1999); adaptive sample size (Bauer and Kohne 1994, Cui, Hung and Wang 1999, Lehmacher and Wassmer 1999, Chen, DeMets and Lan 2004, Mehta and Pocock 2011); two stage phase 2 designs (Gehan 1961, Fleming 1982, Simon 1989); Bayesian phase 2 monitoring (Thall and Simon 1994, Tan and Machin 2002, Lee and Liu 2008, Zhou and colleagues 2017); backward induction and optimal stopping (Bellman 1957, Arrow, Blackwell and Girshick 1949, Wald 1947, Anscombe 1963, Colton 1963, Berry and Ho 1988, Carlin, Kadane and Gelfand 1998); Goldilocks (Broglio and colleagues 2014); I-SPY 2 (Barker and colleagues 2009, Park and colleagues 2016); DAWN (Jovin and colleagues 2017); GBM AGILE (Alexander and colleagues 2018, Wen and colleagues 2026); CALGB 49907 (Muss and colleagues 2009).

- [Exact backward induction for binary endpoints on a cubic lattice](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayesian_clinical_trials_v1/results.html#backward_induction_states) (Section 15.6.2, page 342; proved): For a two arm binary trial the Bayes optimal stopping rule depends only on the success counts and the stage, so backward induction is exact on a lattice of order T cubed states. First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian Adaptive Clinical Trials: Priors, Thompson Sampling, Predictive Stopping and Backward Induction, manuscript submitted to Statistics in Medicine.

chapters.title: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks when allocation should change as data accrue. It starts with the traditional default of fixed allocation (why one to one, and when unequal allocation is justified), then frames allocation as a bandit problem: exploring and exploiting, Thompson sampling, the Bellman equation, the Gittins index, regret and the Lai and Robbins bound, and why the analogy does not transfer as design advice. It tells the ECMO story (the Harvard two stage trial, the UK collaborative trial, how much the prior matters, what the rule did to information). It sets out the critiques of response adaptive randomization, the case against and the case for with the replies, and reproduces the critique. It explains time trends, the failure that matters most, with simulation and fixes, and when randomization helps with many arms, and gives what the regulators say and practical guidance. Cases: I-SPY 2, REMAP-CAP, BATTLE and SHINE with its Bayesian reanalysis.

chapters.title: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks which dose to carry forward. It starts with the traditional 3+3 design, its operating characteristics by simulation and what six patients can tell you. It then gives model based and model assisted designs: the continual reassessment method, the Bayesian optimal interval design (BOIN), mTPI, mTPI 2 and Keyboard, a comparison, escalation with overdose control, a worked logistic model decision and protocol language. It goes beyond the maximum tolerated dose to efficacy, toxicity and dose optimization: why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents, what the FDA guidance asks, a utility formulation, EffTox and phase 1/2 designs, late onset toxicity and time to event interval designs, and randomized dose comparison. It covers dose response estimation outside oncology by MCP Mod, adaptive enrichment, and seamless phase 2/3 designs. chapters.title: Time-to-Event Endpoints
chapters.summary:
This chapter treats time to event endpoints. It starts with the traditional analysis (Kaplan and Meier, the log rank test and the Cox model), then shows that events are the information, derives the gamma posterior for a hazard, and gives predictive probability in an event driven trial. A section on non proportional hazards covers why the hazard ratio misdescribes a delayed or cure type effect, power loss under a delayed effect, and tests built for such effects (weighted log rank, restricted mean survival time and modestly weighted tests). It ends with regulation and practice, key points and exercises.

chapters.title: Borrowing Information
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how external information can enter a trial without bias. It starts from what the traditional design does with prior data and the traditional objections to external and historical controls, then gives the Bayesian idea: exchangeability and hierarchical models, power priors and the normalized power prior (with a rare disease example that chooses the discount by marginal likelihood), commensurate priors, and meta analytic predictive priors with robust mixtures. It measures borrowing by effective sample size and conflict, and the cost of borrowing in type I error and power under drift. It covers pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A, noninferiority with borrowed information and margin synthesis, indirect comparison through a common comparator (the tirzepatide chain), borrowing across subgroups in basket trials, and a case where borrowing failed (an NSCLC external control). It also covers prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins, and gives a decision guide. Cases: REBYOTA, pediatric belimumab and OPTIMIZER Smart.

chapters.title: Master Protocols and Platform Trials
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how one trial infrastructure can answer many questions. It starts with the cost of separate trials, defines master protocol, basket, umbrella and platform, and describes frequentist multi arm multi stage designs. It does the shared control arithmetic (including the number of false positives), then concurrent and non concurrent controls: the regulatory position, a simulation of the bias, and the Bayesian time machine. It treats multiplicity across arms (FDA, EMA and Bayesian error control) and Bayesian platforms: I-SPY 2 graduation by predictive probability, GBM AGILE as a registration platform, REMAP-CAP domains and response adaptive randomization, the COVID anticoagulation multiplatform and the pragmatic pandemic platforms RECOVERY and PANORAMIC. chapters.title: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials
chapters.summary:
This chapter reconstructs landmark trials to show what a Bayesian design would have changed and what it would have cost. SELECT (semaglutide and cardiovascular events) is the main case: the trial as conducted, three monitoring schemes and SELECT's own design with one error rate, the saving in calendar time and exposure, what the monitoring committee would have seen, and what a committee and a regulator would have had to accept. REWIND (dulaglutide) is the case where the scheduled design wins, with a Bayesian reconstruction and the final data under skeptical priors. SURPASS CVOT is an active comparator with a noninferiority margin, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 a prespecified biomarker strategy with baseline tau strata, and BNT162b2 a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization. The chapter values the saving (events and quality adjusted life years, trial cost, timeline and the acceleration bound), compares the protocol side by side and states the limits of reconstruction.

chapters.title: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
chapters.summary:
This chapter reanalyzes published trials in Bayesian terms from their reported estimates. It starts with the normal approximation and its posterior, then GUSTO (when prior trials disagree with the new one), EOLIA (probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis), ANDROMEDA SHOCK (the same pattern with a hazard ratio) and RECOVERY (subgroups and shrinkage). It states what the four reanalyses share and what a reanalysis can and cannot claim: prespecification, prior choice, the regulator's view, and why a reanalysis is not a new trial. A section on what critics say places the cases in the literature on reanalysis and sets the critique of de Grooth and Cremer (that many priors do not contribute to consensus) beside the skeptical prior as an adversary. It ends with exercises.

chapters.title: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what a Bayesian protocol must say and how to work with regulators. chapters.summary:
This appendix describes the software that accompanies the book. It covers installation (R and the bayestrials package, with its tests), how the package is organized (functions in snake case whose prefix names the part of the book, with one argument convention throughout), a worked example, reproducibility (seeds visible beside every simulation, Monte Carlo error reported with results), the companion lab (an interactive tutorial with modules matching the chapters and a Bayesian trial simulator), and established trial design software in wide use: rpact, gsDesign, RBesT, SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans, BOIN, trialr, adaptr, bcrm, Stan and brms, FACTS and East Horizon, with a brief statement of the purpose of each. The descriptions cover only the purpose of each tool, so the reader should consult the tool's documentation for current features and versions. It contains no results.

#### From the literature

Established software for trial design: rpact and gsDesign for group sequential designs, RBesT for meta analytic predictive priors (Weber and colleagues 2021), SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans for Bayesian sample size (Joseph and colleagues), BOIN for dose finding (Yuan and colleagues), trialr, adaptr, bcrm, Stan and brms for Bayesian models, and the commercial packages FACTS and East Horizon.

#### New results

No new results of this appendix are catalogued.

#### Key terms

software, R, bayestrials, rpact, gsDesign, RBesT, SampleSizeProportions, BOIN, trialr, adaptr, bcrm, Stan, brms, FACTS, East Horizon, reproducibility, simulation seed, companion lab.

results.name: Reproduction of the BNT162b2 beta binomial analysis
results.summary: The statistical analysis plan's beta binomial model with a Beta(0.700102, 1) prior, applied to 8 versus 162 cases, gives a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent of 1 minus 2e-28 and a point estimate of 95 per cent, matching the published interval within a tenth of a point.
results.statement: With the plan's prior $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)$ and $s_1 = 8$ cases in the vaccine arm out of $s = 170$, the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102 + 8, 1 + 162)$. The posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent is $1 - 2\times 10^{-28}$, which clears the final analysis threshold 0.986. The 95 per cent credible interval for vaccine efficacy is about $(90.4\%, 97.6\%)$ and the point estimate is 95.1 per cent (plug in) or 94.9 per cent (posterior median), against the published 95.0 per cent with interval 90.3 to 97.6, without modeling the small difference in surveillance time between the arms.
results.label: res-bnt162b2-reproduction

results.name: The Bayes factor bar exceeds the fixed level bar once information times prior variance passes about 46
results.summary: Against a single unadjusted look, the Bayes rule with a point null asks for more evidence than the fixed level test once the data carry about 46 times the information in the prior.
results.statement: At one sided $\alpha = 0.025$ the fixed level test acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha = 1.96$ (that is, $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge 3.84$), and the Bayes rule with equal prior odds acts, asymptotically, when $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n$ with $L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \approx \log n$. They cross at $n^\ast = e^{3.84} \approx 46$, that is at $I_n\tau^2 \approx 46$ (the exact Gaussian expression gives 41.6), which is $n > 46$ for a unit information prior. At $\tau = 0.25$ on the log hazard ratio scale this needs $I_n > 730$, about 2,900 events (exact crossing 41.6: 666 and about 2,660 events). Beyond the crossing the Bayesian bar against a single unadjusted look is the higher one.
results.label: res-bayes-bar-crossing

results.name: Moderate deviation sample size equation
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: A Bayes rule whose bar grows like the logarithm of the sample size has an implicit sample size equation, the textbook formula with the critical value replaced by the square root of log n plus a constant.
results.statement: For the moderate deviation rule, which acts when $Z_n^2 \ge \log n + C$ (with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim), the power against an effect $\theta$ with information $I$ per unit of $n$ is $\Phi\big(\sqrt{nI}\,|\theta| - \sqrt{\log n + C}\big) + o(1)$. Setting this equal to $1-\beta$ gives the sample size equation $n I \theta^2 = \big(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\big)^2$, which is the textbook equation with $z_\alpha$ replaced by $\sqrt{\log n + C}$. The formula is an asymptotic approximation; it is not claimed to predict the size of any particular trial, including SELECT, whose planned size (1,225 events for a design hazard ratio of 0.83; the textbook formula gives about 1,211) is close to the textbook calculation at its own design alternative.
results.label: res-md-sample-size

results.name: Moderate deviation and textbook sizes at the SELECT hazard ratio of 0.80 (not a prediction of SELECT's size)
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: At a hazard ratio of 0.80 and 90 per cent power the textbook formula gives 844 events and the moderate deviation formula more; SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83, where the textbook formula gives about 1,211 events against the planned 1,225, so the formula does not predict SELECT's size.
results.statement: For a hazard ratio of 0.80 ($|\log\mathrm{HR}| = 0.2231$, $Z = |\log\mathrm{HR}|\sqrt{d}/2$ in terms of $d$ events) and 90 per cent power, the textbook calculation at one sided 0.025 calls for 844 events, and the moderate deviation calculation calls for 1,067 events at equal prior odds and 1,255 at prior odds of two to one against. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 per cent power, one sided 0.025 and 1,225 planned events, with one interim at two thirds of them (Ryan et al. 2020), and the observed hazard ratio was 0.80 on 1,270 events (Lincoff et al. 2023). The textbook calculation at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the plan, so the comparison at 0.80 changes the design alternative and does not show that the moderate deviation formula predicts or explains SELECT\'s size.
results.label: res-md-select-prediction

results.name: Four operation ulcer example, adjusted p value against posterior probability
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: In the four operation ulcer example the Bonferroni adjusted p value for best against worst is 0.0855, while the hierarchical posterior probability that drainage is worse than 75 per cent resection is 0.952 on a contrast shrunk from 1.053 to 0.464.
results.statement: In the four operation ulcer example (counts illustrative, at the scale of the 1965 trial of Novick and Grizzle), the Bonferroni adjusted $p$-value for best against worst is $0.0855$, while the hierarchical posterior probability that drainage and vagotomy is worse than 75 per cent resection is $0.952$, on a contrast shrunk from $1.053$ to $0.464$. A posterior probability of $0.952$ is not a claim of statistical significance under strong familywise error control.
results.label: res-ulcer-reading

results.name: The three deviation scales (evidence tolls)
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: A fixed level test, a Bayes rule and an anytime valid rule act at three different sizes of the squared standardized score; for the normal mixture the anytime valid bar exceeds the Bayes bar by a surcharge that is about 2 log(1/alpha) at large information.
results.statement: Let $Z_n$ be the standardized score at information $I_n$, $q = I_n\tau^2$ for a normal prior of scale $\tau$, and $L_n = \log(1+q)$ the Ockham penalty. The one sided fixed level test at level $\alpha$ acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha$. For the symmetric normal mixture, the exact Bayes factor rule with threshold $b$ acts when $Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\}$ with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim, and the anytime valid rule at level $\alpha$ is the same with $b = 1/\alpha$. In the large information approximation these bars are $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log b$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha)$, so that the anytime valid rule requires about $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ more, in squared standardized units, than the Bayes rule at $b = 1$ (exactly $7.38(1 + 1/q)$). This is a property of the normal mixture construction and not a universal cost of anytime validity: other e processes, such as iterated logarithm confidence sequences, behave differently.
results.label: res-evidence-tolls

results.name: The surcharge for validity at every stopping time is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement, as a comparison of boundary terms
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: For the normal mixture e value rule, against the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar (posterior odds of one), the large information surcharge 7.38 is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial standardized requirement 10.51; this compares boundary terms and is not an exact sample size identity.
results.statement: With per observation standardized effect $\theta$, the information needed to act satisfies, in the large information approximation, $n_{\mathrm{MD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{MD}} + C$ for the Bayes rule and $n_{\mathrm{LD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{LD}} + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$ for the anytime valid rule. Subtracting gives $(n_{\mathrm{LD}} - n_{\mathrm{MD}})\theta^2 = 2\log(1/\alpha) + \log(n_{\mathrm{LD}}/n_{\mathrm{MD}})$, and the last term is positive. On the standardized scale the surcharge $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ at $\alpha = 0.025$ is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement $(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2 = 10.51$ at 90 per cent power ($7.38/10.51 \approx 0.70$). This compares boundary terms asymptotically. It is not an exact sample size identity (at $\theta = 0.20$ and $C = 0$ the larger roots differ by about 80 per cent of the fixed requirement), and the exact surcharge is $7.38(1 + 1/q)$. The baseline is the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar; a calibrated Bayesian rule has already paid part of the surcharge, so calibration narrows the realized gap.
results.label: res-seventy-percent

results.name: Calibration of a posterior probability rule by the null maximum
results.summary: The smallest threshold that holds a monitored posterior probability rule to level alpha is the (1 minus alpha) quantile of the largest posterior probability reached over the looks in null simulations, so one simulation serves every threshold.
results.statement: Let $M$ be, for one simulated null trial, the largest posterior probability $\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > a \mid \text{data})$ that the trial reaches at any look it attends. The rule "success if the probability exceeds $c$ at any look" rejects exactly when $M > c$, so its type I error is $\Pr(M > c)$, and the smallest $c$ with type I error at most $\alpha$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$. The $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$ over the null simulations is a Monte Carlo estimate of it: it fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample and not the population error (the binomial standard error near 0.025 is about 0.0008 at 40,000 runs), so the threshold should be validated on independent null simulations. A single simulation serves every candidate $c$ (common random numbers). If futility stopping is part of the design, $M$ is the maximum over the looks the trial actually reaches.
results.label: res-null-max-calibration

results.name: Exact backward induction for binary endpoints on a cubic lattice
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian Adaptive Clinical Trials: Priors, Thompson Sampling, Predictive Stopping and Backward Induction, manuscript submitted to Statistics in Medicine.
results.summary: For a two arm binary trial the Bayes optimal stopping rule depends only on the success counts and the stage, so backward induction is exact on a lattice of order T cubed states.
results.statement: For fixed prior parameters and horizon $T$ pairs, in a two arm trial with binary outcomes and independent beta priors, the optimal policy at stage $k$ is a function of $(s_1, s_0, k)$ only, where $s_1$ and $s_0$ are the success counts in the two arms, and the Bellman recursion evaluates $\sum_{k=0}^{T}(k+1)^2 = (T+1)(T+2)(2T+3)/6 = O(T^3)$ states, each in constant time.
results.label: res-backward-induction-states

results.name: A utility only backward induction rule declares treatment better half the time under the null
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian Adaptive Clinical Trials: Priors, Thompson Sampling, Predictive Stopping and Backward Induction, manuscript submitted to Statistics in Medicine.
results.summary: A stopping loss that does not penalize false positives gives a good treatment choice rule and a useless confirmatory rule, because it declares treatment better in about half of null trials.
results.statement: In the calculation of Polson and Sokolov with $\kappa = 0.0005$ and a maximum of 100 pairs, utility only backward induction declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null (Monte Carlo standard error 0.005) and 0.98 at the large effect, with an expected sample size of 14.4 per arm. The classification loss version with $\gamma = 0.975$ has a null declaration probability of 0.026, power 0.903 and an expected sample size of 54.3 per arm at the large effect. This is a simulation result for the stated loss, prior and horizon.
results.label: res-utility-only-null

results.name: Shared control false positive counts for four arms
results.summary: With a shared control, the chance of at least one false positive among four null arms falls from 9.6 to 7.8 per cent and the chance of two or more rises from 0.4 to 1.7 per cent, while the mean count stays at 0.10.
results.statement: For four null arms each tested at one sided level 0.025, four independent trials give at least one false positive with probability 9.6 per cent and two or more with probability 0.4 per cent. With a shared control and equal allocation these are 7.8 and 1.7 per cent, and with square root allocation (control $\sqrt{k}$ times an experimental arm) they are 8.6 and 1.2 per cent. The mean count is 0.10 in every case. The shared control values are Monte Carlo (400,000 draws).
results.label: res-shared-control-counts

results.name: SELECT reconstruction, median events at decision with conditioning
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Sokolov (2026), Bayesian versus Standard Clinical Trial Design: Theory, Evidence, and Protocol, working paper.
results.summary: In our reconstruction of SELECT at hazard ratio 0.80, a calibrated Bayesian rule stops at a median of 464 events among trials that declare efficacy and 486 over all trials, against 817 for SELECT's planned design (one interim analysis with Lan-DeMets spending, then the final); the e value rule and a four look design are slower or less powerful.
results.statement: In the SELECT reconstruction (true hazard ratio 0.80, normal prior of scale 0.25 on the log hazard ratio, at most 1,270 events, rules evaluated at every second event, 40,000 simulated paths, SELECT designed for hazard ratio 0.83 with 90 per cent power, 1,225 planned events and one interim at two thirds, Ryan et al. 2020), the median number of events at decision among simulated trials that declare efficacy is 464 for the Bayesian rule calibrated to 2.5 per cent one sided, 612 for the e value rule and 952 for a hypothetical four look O\'Brien-Fleming design. Over all trials, counting a trial that never crosses at its maximum, the medians are 486, 714 and 952. Power is 0.947, 0.831 and 0.977, and the realized one sided type I errors are 0.025, 0.0058 and 0.0255 (the Bayesian rule is calibrated to 2.5 per cent, the e value rule is bounded by it). SELECT\'s planned design (interim at 817 of 1,225 events with Lan-DeMets O\'Brien-Fleming type spending, then final) has median 817 in both senses, power 0.974 and type I error 0.0254. A single unadjusted look would cross at 309 events on the mean path, a mean path approximation and not a stopping time. The reconstruction is ours and not the sponsor\'s, and it is a counterfactual, not a power calculation made before the trial.
results.label: res-select-reconstruction
